papers.introduction: The study describes developing and implementing a DLTP to measure and compare adolescent girls' knowledge and skills about digital tools, their importance and practical use, across three phases.
papers.methodology: Quasi-experimental design with adolescent girls aged 14–19 years in eight blocks of District Gumla, Jharkhand (six intervention, two comparison), 2017-2020. Intervention vs comparison samples were 314 vs 272 at baseline, 318 vs 260 at midline and 402 vs 202 at endline. Villages were chosen by proportional random sampling, and girls by systematic random sampling. In-person semi-structured questionnaire (CAPI); face and content validity were established by experts. Univariate analysis and chi-square tests (P < 0.05) were used.
papers.theory: The study uses a five-element digital literacy framework to group questions and score digital literacy, and to design the curriculum.
papers.results: The share above the median did not differ by arm at baseline. It was higher in intervention girls at midline (63.8%, n=203 vs 41.2%, n=107) and endline (90%, n=362 vs 41.6%, n=84), p=0.00 in both. Knowledge and uptake of government schemes was 60.2% (n=242) vs 32.7% (n=66) at endline (p=0.00). Perceived physical security and mass media exposure did not differ significantly at baseline or midline.
papers.discussion: Authors conclude the programme led to improved digital literacy scores in intervention blocks versus comparison blocks, which in turn led to greater awareness and uptake of government schemes. They say the change cannot be attributed completely to the programme, as household possessions also rose, and could not verify links to scheme uptake or economic conditions. They note loss to follow-up. A felt need exists to scale up tailor-made programmes to bridge the digital divide.

abstract_claims.q: For bridging this gap, the physical access to information and communications technology (ICT) along with training to harness these skills is important.
This would empower the girls to gain more control over their health, finances, and safety, and can more freely assert their voice and agency.
The project was implemented in eight blocks of District Gumla of Jharkhand for three years from 2017-2020.
A quantitative questionnaire was developed to collect data from school dropout girls of 10–19 years.
Majority of the participants were unmarried, lived along their parents and had ever attended school in both intervention and comparison arm.
There was no significant difference in the proportion of girls having digital literacy score above median between intervention and comparison arm at the baseline.
At the midline, the proportion of these girls with above median score was significantly higher in the intervention arm
Similarly, at the endline, the proportion of girls with higher median score for digital literacy increased significantly in the intervention arm

The proportion of girls continuing education, physical access to ICT devices at home, exposure to mass media and perceived physical security increased in the intervention arm at the midline and endline as compared to comparison arm in the baseline.
A significantly higher proportion of girls had knowledge about government schemes in the intervention arm as compared to comparison arm at the endline (p<0.05).
We conclude that such tailor-made training programs which are weaved within cultural contexts can effectively bridge the digital gaps in resource scare settings.
Along with this, they have the potential to bridge the literacy and economic gaps also within the community.

Around 29% of girls scored >10 in the intervention arm as opposed to 9% in the comparison arm for the perceived physical security parameter.

Albeit, we cannot attribute this change completely to implementation of this DLTP only as we observed that there was a significant increase in the total household possessions at the midline and endline as compared to baseline, which might have contributed to improved digital literacy.

We could not verify in the community that the increase in household possessions could be due to improved uptake of government schemes which might have resulted in a improving economic conditions of the families.

Since it was a social sector intervention study, so sample coverage and distribution got different across rounds for intervention and comparison arms which are an integral part of any community-based research.
It was difficult for us to assign the intervention randomly in the chosen area of District Gumla in Jharkhand- most of the population is tribal and represent marginalized caste groups.
In the initial phase of the project, it was extremely difficult to convince the families to send their school dropout girls to be a part of this DLTP.
Hence, there was loss-to-follow-up in the project.
Also, the girls got married off which further led to change in population across midline and endline.
Hence, we tried our best to keep the background characteristics similar in the intervention and control arm across the baseline, midline and endline.
When we started this project, a digital literacy program was already in place by Google.
Some of the school going girls became school dropouts and got enrolled in our program by the time we rolled out the intervention.
So, it was practically very difficult to assess whether the improvement in outcomes was totally attributable to our program or was a combination of multiple projects operational in that area.

These can be considered limitations of the current study but controlling strict conditions in such scenarios is not possible owing to social ethics of not depriving anyone of the benefits of training program.
Due to this reason, we could not apply advanced statistics to quantify the impact of DLTP.
Another limitation could be that we could evaluate five elements of DL but the collaborative and productive elements could not be assessed.
So for evaluating these components, a study with long follow up period may be designed to see the impact of DLTP on these two elements.
A lot of programmatic and functional challenges along with sustainability issues were encountered while rolling out DLTP.

papers.introduction: The study aimed to test whether a 6-week digital literacy and digital wellbeing program was associated with more favorable pre-to-post changes in PIU, DSE and DGI than a wait-list control. A second aim tested whether post-intervention data were statistically consistent with a serial pathway from condition through DSE and DGI to PIU.
papers.methodology: Two-arm pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with 206 adolescents aged 12–18 in Hubei Province, China, allocated by quota to an intervention group (n = 103) or a wait-list control group (n = 103). Delivered in person at a community center in March and April 2026. Measures were the SPIUT, the Internet Self-Efficacy subscale of the AIAS, and the short-form DGI. Analysis used 2 × 2 repeated-measures ANOVA and PROCESS Model 6 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples.
papers.theory: The I-PACE model was used to inform the intervention logic. The DSE, DGI and PIU sequence is described as theory-informed, yet still a theoretical proposition.
papers.results: Group × Time interactions were significant for PIU, DSE and DGI (DGI: F(1, 204) = 26.53, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.115). PIU decreased in both groups, more in the intervention group. DGI findings warrant caution: DGI dispersion increased markedly, particularly in the wait-list group, and its source cannot be determined. The standardized serial indirect effect was significant (β = −0.478); the direct effect on PIU was not significant.
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that the program was associated with more favorable self-reported changes in PIU, DSE and DGI than a wait-list condition, and call the findings preliminary and hypothesis-generating. They name non-random allocation, a wait-list that did not control for attention or expectancy, and self-reported outcomes as limitations. They suggest digital literacy education may benefit from moving beyond one-time informational sessions.

Second, the wait-list condition did not control for attention, expectancy, facilitator contact, or general self-monitoring.
Active-control comparisons are needed to distinguish program-specific associations from these nonspecific influences.
Third, DSE, DGI, and PIU were measured concurrently at posttest.
The significant serial indirect association therefore does not establish that DSE changed before DGI or that DGI subsequently reduced PIU.

papers.introduction: The study aims to describe lower secondary technology teachers' experiences of teaching digital models using digital tools. The research question asks how these teachers experience teaching digital models.
papers.methodology: Twelve technology teachers, five males and seven females, were strategically chosen. Semi-structured interviews were chosen, guided by a question guide, lasting 35 to 60 minutes and recorded digitally. All were conducted by the first author in October 2018 and September 2019. A thematic analysis was used. The study was conducted in Swedish lower secondary schools.
papers.theory: The study takes a phenomenological lifeworld approach as its ontological and epistemological basis. ‘Experience’ is its analytic concept.
papers.results: Four themes were found: Enhancing and integrating other subjects; Visualizing technology to the pupils; Enabling digital modelling; and Preparing pupils for the future. The themes partly overlap. Teaching content and methods may differ. The synthesis indicates that teachers did not experience digital models as one single idea but as an amalgam of multiple ideas.
papers.discussion: The overall result is that there is not one way to experience digital models, and therefore not one way to teach them. A conclusion is that discussion of this area needs to be more nuanced and specific to build a common knowledge base. Another topic for further research can be how digital models affect pupils' learning or interest in technology.

papers.introduction: The study aims to examine whether prospective teachers’ use of DVRs affects their TPACK. It asks about the impact on TPACK and its seven domains (TK, PK, CK, PCK, TCK, TPK, TPACK).
papers.methodology: Quasi-experimental pre- and post-survey design with experimental and control groups, plus a descriptive qualitative strand. Sample: 70 prospective teachers, 35 per group, at Al-Qasmi Academic College of Education in Baqa, Israel; sampling was purposive. Instruments: a 53-item self-report TPACK questionnaire and semi-structured interviews with 10 experimental-group teachers. Analysis: Quade’s test, paired-sample t-test, thematic analysis.
papers.theory: The study uses the TPACK framework as both a conceptual foundation and an analytical tool for exploring prospective teacher knowledge in a digital recording environment.
papers.results: Experimental group generally had higher mean scores than the control group on the TPACK components. Quade’s test found group differences significant in all domains, p = 0.001 (TK: F = 23.144, n2 = 0.254). Paired t-tests showed the experimental group improved significantly, while the control group did not. Interviewees reported that DVRs had a significant positive impact on TPACK.
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that DVR use had a significant and positive impact on TPACK in favor of the experimental group. The interviews showed the recordings allowed prospective teachers to reflect and ponder on their teaching skills and content delivery. The authors recommend DVR use by prospective and in-service teachers and adoption of the TPACK model. Stated limitations: no unified control or experimental group; self-reported responses.

introduction.q: The current study aims to answer the following research questions:
this study aims to examine whether the use of DVRs by prospective teachers affects their Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)
What is the impact of prospective teachers’ use of DVRs on their Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) and its seven domains: (TK, PK, CK, PCK, TCK, TPK, TPACK)?

methodology.q: the researcher adopted a quasi-experimental design, utilizing a pre-survey and post-survey design with two groups: experimental and control
For the qualitative strand, a descriptive approach was employed for data collection and analysis.
The study involved a sample of 70 prospective teachers at Al-Qasmi Academic College of Education.
The college is in Baqa, Israel
The sampling was purposive.
The number of prospective teachers in each of the experimental and control groups was 35 prospective teachers.
The present research utilized a self-report questionnaire for the TPACK domains and subdomains
The questionnaire consisted of 53 items
semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 prospective teachers from the experimental group
Quade’s Distribution-Free Test was used
a paired-sample t-test was used
Using Thematic Analysis included six steps

theory.q: This study employed the TPACK framework as both a conceptual foundation and an analytical tool for exploring prospective teacher knowledge within the context of a digital recording environment.
In this study, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework was used as a conceptual framework.
theory.loc: 2.3. The TPACK Framework as a Conceptual Framework

results.q: Generally, the experimental group had higher mean scores in the TPACK components than the control group.
Table 5 shows that the differences in the mean scores of TPACK domains, and between the experimental and control groups, are significant.
Table 6 shows that the participants in the experimental group improved significantly their perceptions of TPACK domains, while those in the control group did not.
The participating prospective teachers reported that using DVRs had a significant positive impact on the development of TPACK.

discussion.q: the use of DVRs by teachers had a significant and positive impact on TPACK in favor of the experimental group
The interviews showed that the recordings allowed the prospective teachers to reflect and ponder on their teaching skills and content delivery.
The quantitative and qualitative results indicate that the use of DVRs by prospective and in-service teachers is recommended
We recommend the adoption of the TPACK model to guide the education of prospective teachers
The main limitation was the inability to provide a unified control group and a unified experimental group, especially since practical training groups are small groups.
Another limitation is the self-reported responses on the questionnaire related to the TPACK domains.

abstract_claims.q: Analyzing digital video recordings (DVRs) is an effective instructional strategy for professionally preparing and developing prospective teachers.
The quantitative and qualitative results showed that prospective teachers in the experimental group significantly and positively impacted TPACK and its seven domains.

The results of the study indicated that digital video recordings allowed prospective teachers to reflect and ponder on their teaching skills, content delivery, and the appropriate use of technology and its relevant tools in the educational process to identify strengths for development and weaknesses for improvement.

Therefore, the results of the current study provide concrete evidence for the need to use DVRs as a promising educational approach in future professional preparation and to develop prospective teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK).
